title: State and metro employment: Third quarter 2026
gist: US nonfarm employment grew 0.4% year over year in Q3 2026, a slight acceleration, with 40 states adding jobs, 10 losing them, and growth accelerating in 37 states versus Q2. South Carolina (+2.3%) led and the District of Columbia (-3.6%) lagged; metro-level growth was weaker (median MSA +0.3%) and noisier, so the St. Louis Fed cautions against over-reading MSA data.

themes.theme: National and state job growth Q3 2026

insights.claim: US national employment growth accelerated slightly to 0.4% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, and the median state also saw job growth of roughly 0.4%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Sub-1% payroll growth signals a slow-but-positive labor market; a late-cycle, low-hiring backdrop relevant to Fed policy and cyclicals.
insights.quote: National employment growth in the third quarter of 2026 accelerated slightly to 0.4% compared to one year ago.
insights.locator: National employment growth in the third quarter

insights.claim: In Q3 2026, 10 US states lost jobs year over year while the remaining 40 grew, showing wide dispersion beneath a modest 0.4% national employment growth rate.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Regional dispersion matters for state munis, regional banks and geographically concentrated REITs/retailers even when the national aggregate looks stable.
insights.quote: state-level results display wider variation, with 10 states losing jobs while the remaining 40 grew strongly compared to one year ago
insights.locator: National employment growth in the third quarter

insights.claim: Year-over-year employment growth accelerated in 37 US states between the second and third quarter of 2026, indicating broad-based momentum improvement.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Breadth of acceleration (37 of 50 states) argues against an imminent broad labor-market downturn.
insights.quote: growth accelerated in 37 states between the second and third quarter
insights.locator: National employment growth in the third quarter

insights.claim: South Carolina and Utah had the strongest state employment growth in Q3 2026, with year-over-year net job gains of 2.3% and 1.4%, respectively.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Sunbelt/Mountain West outperformance supports regional housing, banks and consumer demand in those states.

insights.claim: The District of Columbia had the largest year-over-year net job loss among states in Q3 2026 at 3.6%, followed by Montana at 0.8%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A 3.6% job drop in DC is an outsized local shock; watch DC-area office real estate, local consumer spending and municipal revenues.

insights.claim: US metro-area job growth was slightly weaker than state-level data in Q3 2026, with the median MSA posting a 0.3% year-over-year job gain.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Median metro growth trailing states suggests hiring is concentrated in fewer areas.
insights.locator: At the metro level, job growth

insights.claim: In Q3 2026 the Sandusky, Ohio, MSA had the strongest year-over-year job growth at 4.4%, while the Bloomington, Indiana, MSA had the largest net job loss at 3.4%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Extreme metro readings are likely noisy; treat them as leads to verify rather than trading signals.
insights.locator: At the metro level, job growth

insights.claim: Metro-level (MSA) employment estimates vary greatly from quarter to quarter and carry larger sampling errors than state and national data, so individual MSA readings should not be over-interpreted.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Discount single-quarter MSA prints in regional models; prefer state/national data or multi-quarter averages.
insights.quote: So, be careful not to read too much into these data.
insights.locator: At the metro level, job growth

insights.claim: State and metro job-growth maps can be built in FRED from total nonfarm employees series by setting units to percent change from year ago, quarterly frequency with end-of-period aggregation, and a three-bucket user-defined color scheme (<=0, below 0.7%, and above).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A quick, free way to monitor regional labor-market breadth each quarter.
